doc.title: Stanley Dance interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: Jazz as art form, dancing, and moving too fast
summary: Dance says jazz lost dancers to rock and roll as it became ambitious, comments on Gioia's history, and agrees jazz moved too fast, citing Miles.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Good advice. What do you think of the state of jazz today? It has been kind of elevated to an art form. It’s been institutionalized in colleges and so forth. Do you think it’s a positive thing for the music?
Well it’s hard, I don’t know, it’s very hard to say I think. You see one of the things that was really very important for jazz, and it appears we’ve mainly been talking about, is the

fact that people were dancing to it. And the musicians all liked that, most of them liked it because you know, they are not, it isn’t quite the same thing as an audience sitting down where you’ve got to — I mean that’s why the tempos are so bad on many of those Jazz at the Philharmonic, because the tempos are too fast and they’re just tricks — flamboyant things. You notice how often they’ll repeat a little catchy phrase, and they know this, it’s not really clever but it gets a big hand. It’s a different thing. Well I mean I don’t know that of course rock & roll comes along and takes away — the kids are dancing to rock & roll, partly because jazz had become so ambitious that it wasn’t very danceable. You could dance to it but it didn’t make you want to dance. I think that’s an important difference you know.
I like that word “ambitious” that you just used.

Well it is, isn’t it? Even today. There’s a new book called The History of Jazz by Ted Gioia. Well the first half of it takes you up to the end of the Swing Era and I can understand that, and he’s done a good job. Then when he goes into the rest of the history of jazz, you get bebop, but the later period it seems as though you could do anything and if it’s different, it’s good. But that’s not true you know.
If it’s new then it’s justifiable.
I’ve often felt that jazz has moved too fast for its own good.
You know? Like Miles was a perfect example. As soon as he had people with him, he was off somewhere else.

And then I mean to more or less end up with compromising his world was rather a sign of defeat to my mind. I mean that was a matter of money you could say, but I don’t think it was purely money with him, I think it was kind of desperation.
